summary: Describes the preferred design of a Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge control word for use over an MPLS network, along with the pseudowire associated channel header. The fields are chosen so a label switching router that inspects payloads will not mistake a pseudowire payload for an IP packet. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A small marker at the front of a package so routers that peek inside do not mistake a wrapped old-style message for ordinary internet mail.

questions: what is a pseudowire control word
why does mpls pseudowire start with 0000
how does pseudowire sequence numbering work
what is the pw associated channel header
subtitle: A four-bit marker at the front of pseudowire packets so MPLS routers never mistake them for IP.

tldr.problem: MPLS has no protocol identifier, so a router that peeks at the payload (for example to load-balance) can mistake a pseudowire packet for an IP packet and send its packets down different paths, misordering them.
tldr.mechanism: A pseudowire packet starts with a control word whose first four bits are 0000 (data) or a channel header whose first four bits are 0001, values that can never look like IPv4 or IPv6. The preferred control word also carries a length and a 16-bit sequence number.
tldr.outcome: Routers can tell pseudowire traffic from IP, and receivers can detect misordering. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 5586.

today: RFC 4385 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 5586. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem: Pseudowires Look Like IP
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) carries some other kind of traffic across an MPLS packet switched network (PSN). Standard MPLS encapsulations have no explicit protocol identifier, so a label switching router (LSR) that performs MPLS payload inspection has to guess what is inside a packet.

One example is an LSR doing equal-cost multiple-path load balancing (ECMP, see RFC 2992). If it treats a PW packet as IP, the packets of one PW may follow different paths and arrive misordered at the egress provider edge (PE). Splitting paths can also stop the PW's OAM mechanism from monitoring it correctly.

This RFC specifies how the PW control word tells a PW payload apart from an IP payload, and gives the preferred control word layout and the PW Associated Channel Header. The architecture of pseudowires itself is in RFC 3985.
sections.eli5: Some routers peek inside packages to decide which road to use. If they get fooled, a stream of packages can split up and arrive in the wrong order. This RFC adds a label that stops them being fooled.

sections.title: Avoiding ECMP by Choosing the First Nibble
sections.content:
All IP packets start with a version number that LSRs doing payload inspection check. So PW packets over MPLS MUST NOT start with the value 4 (IPv4) or 6 (IPv6) in the first nibble, because those are assumed to carry normal IP.

The RFC defines a PW header with two general formats. The PW MPLS Control Word (PWMCW) is for data passing over the PW, and the PW Associated Channel Header (PWACH) is for functions such as OAM. A first nibble of 0 means the packet starts with a PWMCW; a first nibble of 1 means it starts with a PWACH. Any other first nibble value for a PW packet is deprecated.

If a PW is sensitive to misordering and the PSN uses payload contents to pick an ECMP path, the PW MUST use a mechanism that prevents misordering. The PWMCW or PWACH MUST immediately follow the bottom of the MPLS label stack.
sections.eli5: The first digit on the label says what kind of package it is. Zero means ordinary pseudowire data and one means a special message, and neither can ever be confused with internet mail.

sections.title: The Generic and Preferred Control Word
sections.content:
The generic PWMCW is just a first nibble of 0000 followed by 28 bits that are specified by the PW encapsulation. Whether a PW uses a control word is decided by the PW set-up protocol or by configuration. Any control word MUST follow this generic format, and SHOULD follow the preferred format so that different PW types stay consistent.

The preferred format has these fields after the leading nibble:

  • Flags (bits 4 to 7): MAY be used for per-payload signaling. Their meaning MUST be defined in the PW specification.
  • FRG (bits 8 and 9): used when fragmenting a PW payload. The RFC points to a work in progress for the details, and says these bits may serve as general purpose flags if the PW type never needs fragmentation.
  • Length (bits 10 to 15): lets the receiving PE strip padding that an Ethernet segment may have added. If the MPLS payload is less than 64 bytes it MUST be the length of the PW payload plus the control word; otherwise it MUST be zero.
  • Sequence number (bits 16 to 31): used for sequencing.
sections.eli5: The label has a few small boxes: some free-to-use switches, a note for when a big parcel is cut into pieces, a size to ignore extra stuffing, and a counter number.

sections.title: Sequencing Rules
sections.content:
The sequence number mechanism is specific to each PW. The PW encapsulation specification may define its own or say that the one in this RFC is used. The mechanism here uses a circular unsigned 16-bit number space that excludes zero.

Sender. If sequencing is supported and enabled, the first packet is sent with sequence number one and each later packet adds one. After 65535 the next number is one. If the sender does not support sequencing or it is disabled, the field MUST be zero in every packet.

Receiver. The expected sequence number starts at one. For each packet:

  • A sequence number of zero means order cannot be determined, so the packet is treated as in order.
  • A number equal to the expected one is in order.
  • A number ahead of the expected one by less than 32768, or behind it by 32768 or more (the wrap-around case), is inside the allowed window, and the implementation MAY treat it as in order.
  • Anything else is out of order.

After a non-zero packet the expected number becomes that packet's number plus one, wrapping from 65535 to one. Out-of-order packets MAY be dropped or reordered, at the receiver's discretion. A PE that negotiated not to use receive sequence processing but gets a non-zero sequence number SHOULD send a PW status message indicating a receive fault and disable the PW. A non-normative appendix gives pseudo-code for all this.
sections.eli5: Number the packages 1, 2, 3 and so on, and start again at 1 after the biggest number. The receiver knows which one it wants next, so it notices if one is missing or late. Zero means we are not counting.

sections.title: The PW Associated Channel Header
sections.content:
Some PW features need an associated channel: a channel multiplexed into the PW with user traffic, so that it follows the same path through the PSN. Over MPLS it is identified by a four-byte header whose first nibble is 0001. This lets it be told apart both from an IP packet and from a PW data packet.

  • Version: the RFC defines version 0.
  • Reserved: MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on reception.
  • Channel Type: 16 bits, defined in an IANA registry.
sections.eli5: This is a separate lane for special notes that rides along inside the same stream of packages, so it always takes exactly the same road.

sections.title: The Channel Type Registry
sections.content: IANA has set up a registry of Pseudowire Associated Channel Types. The values are 16 bits and are assigned by the IETF Consensus policy. Two values are named in the RFC: 0x21 means the associated channel carries an IPv4 packet, and 0x57 means it carries an IPv6 packet.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of numbers saying what kind of special note each channel holds, such as one number for each kind of internet mail.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The associated channel can potentially be misused. Any application using it MUST consider the resulting security issues and provide mechanisms to stop an attacker from disrupting the PW or the PE, or from using the channel to deliver packets elsewhere. Choosing the mechanism is outside the scope of this document.

If a PW is configured to operate without a control word, the PW Associated Channel Type mechanism MUST NOT be used. Otherwise user payloads could be crafted to mimic the PWACH and attack the application that uses the associated channel.
sections.eli5: Special notes could be faked, so anyone using them must add protection, and if the label is not used at all, the special lane must not be used either.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Per-payload signaling, defined by the PW specification.

fields.name: FRG
fields.desc: Used when fragmenting a PW payload.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Payload plus control word if the MPLS payload is under 64 bytes, otherwise zero.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Starts at one, wraps from 65535 to one, zero means not used.

fields.desc: Version of the header; this RFC defines version 0.

fields.desc: MUST be sent as 0 and ignored on reception.
